title: Why do Europe’s best defence ideas end up in the US?
content:
A small European company builds a military prototype with EU money. Then it hits a wall of testing, certification, and procurement that can take years. European lawmakers now want to knock that wall down.

The road from prototype to the armed forces can take years, and investors are hard to find along the way. By the time a product reaches the market, military requirements may already have changed. This is one of the problems facing Europe’s defence industry, according to a report the European Parliament adopted on Thursday by 411 votes to 133, with 41 abstentions.

MEPs warn that small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) and start-ups developing defence technologies struggle to turn innovation into operational capabilities. As a result, some promising companies cannot scale up, while others look for investors outside Europe.

Lawmakers identify two critical bottlenecks, which they call ‘valleys of death’. The first separates the development of a technology from its military validation. The second comes after successful testing, when companies still have to find customers willing to buy and deploy their products.

title: Stuck on repeat. How AI recommendations sideline Europe’s artists
content:
Your feed picks the next song. ChatGPT picks the next book. Your streaming service already knows your next series. But the AI behind this easy discovery keeps pushing what is already popular. European artists warn that newcomers and minority-language voices are getting lost.

AI recommendations increasingly shape what we read, watch, and listen to. These systems use data about our preferences, behaviour, or even other users’ interests to suggest what we might enjoy next. But the way they decide what deserves our attention is still very opaque. European artists warn that AI recommendations make the fight for attention harder, particularly for emerging artists.

A recent European Commission study connected the availability and visibility of European cultural works to opaque recommendation algorithms, language barriers, and digital platforms’ tendency to amplify mainstream content. Similarly, a study examining book recommendations in Danish public libraries found that authors from less popular nationalities received up to 40 per cent less exposure.

title: A home of your own? Elusive dream as property prices outpace incomes
content:
The gap between what Europeans earn and what it costs to buy a flat or a house is widening, fuelling a crisis that threatens to spill beyond the housing market.

In Spain, frustration over unaffordable housing erupted this week into one of the biggest protests in recent years. Around four million workers took part in a nationwide general strike, according to trade unions. It was the first of its kind in 14 years. Thousands took to the streets of Madrid, Barcelona and other cities.

Most demonstrations remained peaceful, but clashes with police broke out in some places later in the evening. Rubbish bins were set alight and protesters threw objects at officers.

Spain faces a particularly acute shortage. According to the country’s central bank, it lacks around 750,000 homes. Meanwhile, rising rents are putting growing pressure on households priced out of homeownership.
snippet: The gap between what Europeans earn and what it costs to buy a flat or a house is widening, fuelling a crisis that threatens to spill beyond the housing market.
creator: Anna Marvanová

title: ‘Sovereignty doesn’t mean isolation’: Lawmaker steering EU cloud rules on digital independence
content:
Europe must reduce its reliance on foreign tech giants without shutting itself off from global players, says Diego Solier (ECR/ES), the European Parliament’s rapporteur for the Cloud and AI Development Act. Speaking to EU Perspectives, the lawmaker argues that the EU needs to combine regulatory simplification, faster infrastructure development and stronger public demand to help European cloud providers scale up and compete internationally.

The Cloud and AI Development Act (CADA) aims to boost Europe’s data centre capacity and reduce its reliance on foreign cloud providers. It seeks to do so by streamlining permits, creating demand for European cloud services through public procurement and introducing security requirements for public entities.

Solier’s appointment as rapporteur raised eyebrows in some quarters: a first-term lawmaker, he nevertheless brings a strong IT background to the role.
snippet: Europe must reduce its reliance on foreign tech giants without shutting itself off from global players, says Diego Solier (ECR/ES), the European Parliament’s rapporteur for the Cloud and AI
creator: Jennifer Baker

title: Europe’s industrial heart stalls as Spain and Poland race ahead
content:
Mercedes-Benz halted all further investment in Germany on Thursday. A day later, fresh figures showed the problem runs deeper than one carmaker. Europe’s industrial heart is cooling, hiring has stopped, and the US is now growing twice as fast.

The headline figure looks calm. The eurozone grew by 0.4 per cent between July and September, according to a flash estimate from Eurostat, the EU’s statistics office. That is a little slower than in the spring, but hardly a crisis.

The trouble lies underneath. After a year of small gains, the number of people in work did not grow at all. Meanwhile, the US economy expanded twice as fast as the eurozone’s.

France has become Europe’s problem child. Its economy has not grown in a single quarter this year and is now smaller than a year ago, the only one in the EU. Exports and investment are falling.

French households are still spending. But inflation has climbed to its highest level since early 2024, and rising prices eat into their budgets just as Paris tries to rein in one of Europe’s largest deficits. Every month without growth makes that task harder.

title: ‘Talent has no gender.’ Women are making their way into science but few reach the top
content:
Four in ten science and engineering jobs are held by women, amounting to 8.2 million positions. But the figures hide stark regional differences and a persistent shortage of women in senior research roles.

Women accounted for 41 per cent of the EU’s 20.2 million scientists and engineers in 2025, according to new Eurostat figures. The category extends beyond laboratories and engineering firms to include professionals in health and information technology.

Île-de-France, which includes Paris, employed 336,300 female scientists and engineers, making it the largest number among the broad regions compared. Yet women held just 38 per cent of those jobs, below the EU’s 41 per cent average. In Germany’s North Rhine-Westphalia and Bavaria, the proportion was 35 per cent.

Women formed a majority in ten regions: four in Spain, two in Portugal and one each in Greece, Poland, Sweden and France’s outermost territories. Most had relatively small science and engineering workforces. Spain’s north-east region, Noreste, had the largest female workforce within this group, at 102,700, representing 51 per cent.

title: Industry set for extra free carbon allowances until 2030 as EU negotiators reach agreement
content:
European factories could pay less for their emissions under an EU deal reached on Thursday night. Negotiators agreed to provide around 121 million extra free carbon permits through 2030, following warnings that rising costs could push production abroad. 

“This amendment will provide the predictability industry needs for the sustainable transition, while remaining competitive at home and retaining production within the EU,” Irish Climate Minister Darragh O’Brien said after the provisional agreement. The changes cover 2026–2030.

The measure concerns industrial activities whose free allowances depend on heat and fuel use rather than product-specific benchmarks. These rules cover activities including chemicals, paper, food processing, ceramics and glass. The revision follows complaints about reductions in free allocations after a benchmark update in June. 

Under the emissions trading system, companies must cover their emissions with allowances. Receiving more for free can reduce the number they need to buy. The policy aims to prevent production shifting to countries where competitors face lower carbon costs.

title: Europe’s new medicine law is almost done. Making it work has barely started
content:
New medicines take more than 1,000 days to reach patients in Romania. Pharmacists lose 12 hours a week chasing shortages. The EU’s biggest medicine reform in two decades aims to tackle both, and lawmakers have now cleared it in committee. Industry, regulators, wholesalers, and pharmacists still disagree on what it will change in practice.

The reform has one vote left. Then a two-year clock starts. Industry, regulators, and the supply chain now worry less about the text and more about how 27 countries will apply it.

On 10 November, the European Parliament’s Committee on Public Health (SANT) voted on its recommendation for the second reading of the pharma package. The package consists of a regulation and a directive. MEPs adopted both texts in two roll-call votes. 

“We established improvements for patients for security of supply. We made sure that companies invest in Europe and develop medicines in Europe,” said MEP Tiemo Wölken (S&D/DEU), rapporteur for the regulation. MEP Dolors Montserrat (EPP/ESP) is rapporteur for the directive.

The full Parliament still has to vote. After that, the texts go to the Official Journal.

title: Too soft or too much? Digital Fairness Act divides Brussels
content:
Brussels wants to end subscription traps, hidden fees, and fake low-stock warnings. Consumer groups welcome the Digital Fairness Act, while some MEPs say it should ban addictive design outright. Business, meanwhile, warns of yet another layer of EU rules.

Unveiled on Wednesday, the proposal targets manipulative online practices, known as “dark patterns”, such as fake low-stock warnings, hidden fees, and misleading purchasing options. It also introduces rules on influencer marketing, personalised pricing, addictive design and subscription cancellations. Consumers would also gain more control over features like endless scrolling and autoplay.

Alongside the DFA, the Commission proposed stronger enforcement powers for itself to investigate consumer law breaches and impose fines of up to 6 per cent of global turnover. Unfair online practices cost Europeans €10.3bn a year. The Commission estimates the package could save consumers up to €13.7bn annually.

Reactions from MEPs to the Digital Fairness Act reveal disagreement over how far the EU should go in regulating online businesses. Progressive lawmakers want stronger consumer safeguards, while conservatives warn against more regulation.
snippet: Brussels wants to end subscription traps, hidden fees, and fake low-stock warnings. Consumer groups welcome the Digital Fairness Act, while some MEPs say it should ban addictive design outright.
creator: Joana Soares

title: Putin: Foreign troops in Ukraine would mean another war
content:
A foreign military presence would make any peace deal a recipe for renewed war, Russian president warns. Yet Washington is signalling progress and offering Europe a seat at the table.

Deploying European troops in Ukraine after a peace deal would trigger a resumption of the war, Russian President Vladimir Putin warned on Thursday. He made the remarks during talks with US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner at the Kremlin.

After their meeting in Moscow, the Americans flew to Dublin, where they are due to meet Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. Witkoff also announced that European countries would take part in the next round of peace talks.

During his meeting with the US envoys, Mr Putin reiterated that Moscow considers any foreign military presence in Ukraine unacceptable. “The Europeans are aware of this. And what do we hear from them? That once a peace agreement is signed, they will immediately deploy troops to Ukrainian territory,” he said. “What does this mean? We have already talked about it: for us, they are a legitimate target, meaning the war will resume immediately.”
snippet: A foreign military presence would make any peace deal a recipe for renewed war, Russian president warns. Yet Washington is signalling progress and offering Europe a seat at the table.
creator: Anna Marvanová

title: Faster trials, less red tape. If Europe doesn’t act, patients could miss out on new treatments
content:
Europe risks losing further ground to the US and China in clinical research unless it makes trials faster and easier to run. But improving regulatory timelines will need to go hand in hand with investment in hospitals, better coordination and stronger patient involvement.

The proposed European Biotech Act offers an opportunity to address some of the barriers facing clinical trials in the EU, from fragmented approval procedures to administrative burdens. But participants of a roundtable in the European Parliament cautioned that shortening deadlines on paper will not automatically translate into faster access to innovative treatments.

“Clinical trials are a fundamental part of pharmaceutical innovation. They are essential not only for developing new treatments, but also for ensuring that European patients can participate in research and benefit from medical advances,” said MEP Ondřej Krutílek (ECR/CZE), who hosted the discussion together with the Czech Association of the Innovative Pharmaceutical Industry (AIFP).

title: Europe’s space ambitions meet ferocious resistance over sovereignty
content:
A shield or not a shield, that is the question. Really? Low Earth Orbit, today’s critical defence frontier is rapidly crowding with rival hardware. Yet national self-interest chokes a unified strategy just as the window for action is closing.

Space warfare is already here, and commercial satellites have become legitimate military targets. That is the finding of Challenges to security in space: Congestion, competition, and cooperation 2026, a report by the US Defense Intelligence Agency. It describes space as a contested military domain.

The report names four principal non-allied actors: China, Russia, Iran, and North Korea. They are developing systems to deny an adversary access to space-based services. “Space almost certainly will remain an increasingly competitive and crowded environment as space capabilities improve and other countries seize opportunities in space,” the agency says.

The report counts about 15,058 satellites in low-Earth orbit (LEO) as of this past June. “Russia is currently capable of targeting satellites in LEO with both terrestrial and orbital systems and is interested in developing systems for targeting more distant orbits,” it said.
